# Three fibers with a centrally symmetric middle: an all-dimensional residual bound

This is a theorem for exactly three full-dimensional positive fibers at
the integer bases -1,0,1. Only the middle fiber is assumed centrally
symmetric. The endpoint shapes and positions are arbitrary. It does not
resolve arbitrary integer projections or arbitrary nonsymmetric fibers.

## 1. Statement and the actual two-point selection

Fix d>=1. Let A,K,B be full-dimensional convex bodies in R^d satisfying
(A+B)/2 subset K, and let

    S=({-1} times A) union({0} times K) union({1} times B).

These are actual convex-compatible fibers; for example their convex
hull has exactly these integer fibers and nonempty ambient interior.
Write |A|=a_b, |B|=b, |K|=k_b, and exchange the endpoint labels if
needed so that0<a_b<=b. Assume K is centrally symmetric about c.
All masses below use the actual mixed measure sum_z vol_d(S_z), whose
total is M=a_b+k_b+b. Thus the intrinsic dimension here is q=d.

Set

    Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d,
    rho=((d-1)/(d+1))^d,
    beta_d=Gamma/(1+2Gamma+rho).                     (1)

Then ONE of the two actual points

    Y_0=(0,c),             Y_1=(1,g_B)

has raw ambient halfspace depth at least beta_d M, where g_B is the
ordinary centroid of B. More explicitly normalize

    a=a_b/b in(0,1],       h=k_b/(2b),
    s=(2h^(1/d)-1)_+,
    L=h+(a-s^d)_+.

The two points have respectively the deterministic lower bounds bL
and bGamma. Choose Y_0 when L>=Gamma, and Y_1 otherwise.

Moreover

    beta_d>=Gamma/2,                                (2)

with strict inequality for d>=3. Therefore the n=1 OC inequality
holds for this entire three-fiber class. The displayed two-center
selector has actual sharp examples in every dimension in Section5.
In dimension two beta_2=2/9, in dimension one beta_1=1/4, and for
example beta_3=3/14.
No symmetry of A or B is used in the theorem.

## 2. Endpoint residuals inside the actual missed middle half

Take an arbitrary ambient halfspace through Y_0 whose continuous normal
u is nonzero. Its traces are

    H_-={x:u dot x>=u dot c+alpha},
    H_0={x:u dot x>=u dot c},
    H_+={x:u dot x>=u dot c-alpha}

for some real alpha. Every such alpha is allowed, so these include all
oblique orientations. Let their endpoint captured volumes, divided by
b, be U,V, and put P=U+V. The own middle contribution divided by b is
exactly h, by central symmetry and the null d-volume of hyperplanes.

Define the CLOSED endpoint residuals by reversing the displayed weak
inequalities. Their normalized volumes are a-U and1-V; boundary mass
is zero. Their Minkowski midpoint lies in the closed missed middle
half K intersect{u dot x<=u dot c}, of normalized volume h. Whenever
P<a, both residual volumes are positive. Ordinary Brunn--Minkowski
then gives

    (a-U)^(1/d)+(1-V)^(1/d)<=2h^(1/d).              (3)

There is no replacement of the mixed fiber sum by an integral: (3)
is an ordinary continuous inequality between these three actual sets.

For fixed0<=P<a, the function

    f(U)=(a-U)^(1/d)+(1-P+U)^(1/d),  0<=U<=P,

is concave, so its minimum is at an endpoint. The smaller endpoint
value is f(P)=(a-P)^(1/d)+1. To check the orientation, put q=1/d.
For fixed P, the increment t^q-(t-P)^q decreases with t>=P, because
its derivative is q[t^(q-1)-(t-P)^(q-1)]<=0 (for d=1 it is constant).
Since a<=1,

    a^q-(a-P)^q >= 1-(1-P)^q,

which is exactly f(0)>=f(P). Thus (3) implies

    (a-P)^(1/d)+1<=2h^(1/d).                       (4)

If2h^(1/d)<=1, (4) is impossible when P<a, so P>=a. Otherwise it
implies P>=a-(2h^(1/d)-1)^d. Together with P>=0, and the automatic
validity when P>=a, all statuses give the single formula

    P >= (a-(2h^(1/d)-1)_+^d)_+.                  (5)

This proves the raw lower bound bL for every nonvertical through-Y_0
cap. A pure integer through-Y_0 cap contains the entire middle fiber
and at least one endpoint; its mass is at least b(2h+a)>=bL.
Any merely containing halfspace contains its parallel through-Y_0
halfspace. Consequently the bound covers every closed ambient cap.

The other point Y_1 belongs to B. Ordinary Grunbaum's centroid
inequality, applied only to its own fiber, gives raw depth at least
bGamma for every ambient cap containing Y_1. Pure integer caps retain
the whole own fiber and satisfy this bound as well. This is the only
ordinary centroid theorem used here; no rounding is involved.

## 3. The exact scalar minimum

We prove, for every0<=a<=1 and h>=0,

    max{Gamma,h+(a-s^d)_+}/(1+a+2h)>=beta_d,
    s=(2h^(1/d)-1)_+.                             (6)

First note two elementary dimensional inequalities:

    Gamma<=1/2,              2Gamma+rho<=1.         (7)

For the first, (1+1/d)^d>=2 by the first two binomial terms. For
the second, expand at d:

    (d+1)^d-(d-1)^d
       =2 sum_(j odd) binom(d,j)d^(d-j)
       >=2d^d.

The first odd term j=1 is exactly2d^d; additional terms exist and
are positive precisely when d>=3. Dividing by(d+1)^d proves (7),
including its equality for d=1,2 and strictness for d>=3.

Suppose first0<=h<=Gamma. Write t=s^d. Then0<=t<=rho. At fixed h,
the numerator in (6) is constant Gamma until

    a_0=Gamma-h+t,

and is h+a-t thereafter. This breakpoint lies in[0,1]: it is at
least t, while a_0<=Gamma+rho<=1-Gamma. The constant-numerator
quotient decreases with a; the other quotient increases, since its
derivative has positive numerator1+h+t. Hence its exact minimum
over a is

    Gamma/(1+Gamma+h+t)
        >=Gamma/(1+2Gamma+rho)=beta_d.              (8)

This reasoning includes t=0 and the endpoint a_0=0; no positive
residual was assumed in the scalar optimization.

Suppose next Gamma<=h<=1. Now h>=Gamma, so the outer maximum is
irrelevant. Put t=s^d in[rho,1]. The quotient decreases up to a=t
and increases thereafter, by the same positive derivative1+h+t.
Its minimum is

    h/(1+t+2h).                                    (9)

The inverse relation between t and h is

    h=v(t)=2^(-d)(1+t^(1/d))^d.

This function is concave on[0,1]: expanding the d-th power gives a
nonnegative linear combination of the concave functions t^(j/d),
0<=j<=d. It satisfies v(rho)=Gamma and v(1)=1. The affine function

    ell(t)=Gamma(1+t)/(1+rho)

agrees with v at rho and is at most v at1, since2Gamma<=1+rho.
Concavity of v-ell therefore gives

    h/(1+t)>=Gamma/(1+rho),

throughout[rho,1]. Applying the increasing function x/(1+2x) gives
from (9) the lower bound beta_d.

Finally if h>=1, the numerator is at least h and a<=1, so the
quotient is at least h/(2+2h)>=1/4. Inequality2Gamma<=1+rho gives
1/4>=beta_d. This proves (6) over its entire domain.

The scalar constant is exact: at h=Gamma,a=rho, its numerator is
Gamma and its denominator is1+2Gamma+rho. For d>=2 this has a>0.
For d=1, where rho=0, the same value1/4 also occurs at every
h=(1+a)/2 with0<a<=1. Section5 realizes these equality parameters
with tight actual cap bounds for the specified two-center selector.
No sharpness assertion about the unrestricted global depth follows.

## 4. The theorem and scope of its improvement

Section2 gives max{D_S(Y_0),D_S(Y_1)}>=b max{L,Gamma}. Since
M=b(1+a+2h), (6) proves (1). Every point used is a single actual
mixed-integer point. All cap orientations and boundary statuses were
handled before the scalar optimization. Exchanging the endpoint
labels is the lattice-preserving reflection z maps to -z; scalar
volume normalization divides all masses by the same positive b.

By (7), the denominator1+2Gamma+rho is at most2, proving (2).
It is strictly smaller than2 for d>=3, giving a uniform positive
dimension-dependent improvement over the OC constant in this class.
The conclusion does not assume equal endpoint volumes, affine
centroids, a product structure, or any restriction on the continuous
dimension, but it does assume precisely three positive full-dimensional
fibers and central symmetry of the middle one. Lower-dimensional
fiber intersections and larger integer projections are not included.

## 5. Actual planar equality for the specified two-center selector

Let

    B=conv{(-1,0),(1,0),(0,1)},     A=B/3,
    M_0=(A+B)/2=(2/3)B,
    K=conv(M_0,-M_0).

Then |B|=1, |A|=1/9, and K is the centrally symmetric diamond with
vertices(+-2/3,0),(0,+-2/3), of area8/9. The convex hull of the
three layers is an actual full-dimensional convex body with exactly
these integer fibers. The total mixed area is2.

At the middle symmetry center Y_0=(0,0,0), the own fiber supplies
4/9 in every nonvertical cap. The downward cap with continuous
trace {x_2<=0} captures only boundary edges of A and B, of area zero,
and exactly half of K. Thus D_S(Y_0)=4/9.

At the larger endpoint centroid Y_1=(1,0,1/3), ordinary Grunbaum
supplies4/9. Its upward own cap {x_2>=1/3} has area(2/3)^2=4/9.
A finite positive integer tilt in

    x_2+alpha(z-1)>=1/3

excludes K and A while preserving this trace on B. For example
alpha=1 suffices. Thus D_S(Y_1)=4/9 as well. Both selected points
have normalized depth2/9=beta_2. This proves that the specified
two-center selector cannot have a universally larger planar constant.
No assertion about the global best point of this example is needed.

### The same selector constant is sharp in every dimension

For d>=2, take any centrally symmetric(d-1)-dimensional convex body
D in R^(d-1), centered at zero and of volume d. Let B be the cone
with base D times{0} and apex(0,1). Its sections at height t in[0,1]
are(1-t)D, so Cavalieri gives

    |B|=d integral_0^1 (1-t)^(d-1)dt=1,
    (g_B)_d=d integral_0^1 t(1-t)^(d-1)dt=1/(d+1).

Its other centroid coordinates are zero by the symmetry of D. The
apex cap at height1/(d+1) has volume Gamma. Set

    r=d/(d+1),   t_0=(d-1)/(d+1),
    A=t_0 B,     M_0=rB,     K=conv(M_0,-M_0).

The endpoint midpoint is M_0 because(1+t_0)/2=r. Symmetry of D
makes K exactly the union M_0 union(-M_0): its section at height q
is(r-|q|)D for |q|<=r, a concave radial profile defining a convex
double cone. Consequently

    |A|=rho,       |K|=2Gamma,       |B|=1.

The downward middle cap at c_K=0 captures no endpoint volume and
exactly Gamma from K. Own symmetry gives the reverse lower bound,
so D_S(0,0)=Gamma. At the endpoint centroid, ordinary Grunbaum gives
Gamma. The actual cap

    x_d+(z-1)>=1/(d+1)

retains the apex cap of B and excludes K and A, so its total mass
is exactly Gamma. Thus D_S(1,g_B)=Gamma too. Their best normalized
depth is exactly Gamma/(1+2Gamma+rho)=beta_d.

For d=1 use B=[0,1], A=[0,a] with0<a<=1, and
K=[-(1+a)/2,(1+a)/2]. At its symmetry center the downward cap
shows raw depth exactly(1+a)/2; own symmetry gives the lower bound.
The endpoint centroid has raw depth1/2, by finite isolation and the
ordinary interval bound. The selected maximum divided by total
mass2(1+a) is exactly1/4=beta_1.

These are sharp examples only for the stated choice between c_K
and the ordinary centroid g_B. In dimensions above two, this proof
does not claim that g_B is an ordinary deepest point of the cone,
or that either selected point maximizes the full mixed depth.

## 6. Relation to the earlier density-only obstruction

The example in
candidate 44f410354149993c
has a=4/25, k_b/b=6272/7425 and d=2. Its density-ceiling certificate
falls below the OC target. Formula (5) retains a different actual
constraint: the two endpoint residual convex bodies must fit in the
same missed HALF of the symmetric middle fiber. It is not a new
choice of a density coefficient and it does not assume the unrealized
density extremizer comes from endpoint transport. The all-dimensional
scalar proof above shows that this additional geometry repairs every
volume triple for the stated middle-symmetric three-fiber class.

## 7. Exact extension to an actual ordinary center of an asymmetric middle

The residual argument also identifies precisely what optimizing the
middle's ordinary depth can accomplish without retaining directional
shape data. Now K need not be symmetric. Suppose an actual point c in
K has ordinary normalized halfspace depth at least sigma, where

    Gamma<=sigma<=1/2.

Put

    r=sigma/(1-sigma),
    H=Gamma/r=Gamma(1-sigma)/sigma,
    T=(2H^(1/d)-1)^d,
    beta_d(sigma)=Gamma/(1+Gamma+H+T).              (10)

Here Gamma<=H<=1-Gamma<1 and H>=2^(-d), so the power defining T
has a nonnegative base. One of the actual points (0,c),(1,g_B) has
normalized mixed depth at least beta_d(sigma).

Indeed normalize a=a_b/b and h=(1-sigma)k_b/b. The own cap at c has
mass at least b r h, and its missed mass is at most bh. The exact
same residual argument as Section2 gives the raw bound

    b[rh+(a-(2h^(1/d)-1)_+^d)_+].                  (11)

Pure integer caps again contain the whole middle and an endpoint,
and dominate this bound. The original total is now
b[1+a+(1+r)h]. Thus we must minimize the ratio

    max{Gamma,rh+(a-t)_+}/[1+a+(1+r)h],
    t=(2h^(1/d)-1)_+^d.                            (12)

For0<=h<=H the minimizing a is a_0=Gamma-rh+t. It lies in[0,1]:
t<=h for h<=1, and therefore a_0<=Gamma+(1-r)H=H<=1.
The exact minimum is Gamma/(1+Gamma+h+t), at least (10).
For H<=h<=1 the minimizing a is t. Writing h=v(t) as in Section3,
concavity gives

    h/(1+t)>=H/(1+T).

To verify the endpoint comparison needed here, convexity of x^d
gives v(T)<= (1+T)/2, or2H<=1+T; the other endpoint is t=1.
Substitution yields (10). Finally h>=1 gives a ratio at least
r/(3+r), which is no smaller than (10), again by2H<=1+T.
These three cases prove the assertion. The scalar minimum is exact
at a=T,h=H. It is a minimum of the stated volume/depth certificate,
not automatically the depth of a geometric extremizer.

One may choose c to be an actual ordinary deepest point of K.
Such a point exists: for every fixed nonzero direction, the volume
of the through-x cap is continuous in x because hyperplane boundaries
are null; the infimum over directions is upper semicontinuous on
compact K, hence attains its maximum. Grunbaum ensures that this
maximum is at least Gamma|K|, and complementary through-point caps
bound it above by |K|/2. A deterministic selection can, for example,
minimize the coordinates successively on the compact maximizing set.
No point in conv(S) outside its actual middle fiber is selected.

The exact criterion for (10) to imply OC is

    H+(2H^(1/d)-1)^d<=1-Gamma.                     (13)

The left side is strictly increasing in H. For d=2 it equals
1-Gamma at H=Gamma, so (13) holds only at sigma=1/2. Thus replacing
the prescribed centroid by an ordinary deepest point does not, by
itself, extend this planar volume-only certificate below half-depth.
For d>=3 there is a unique H_c in(Gamma,1-Gamma) where equality
holds; equivalently the sufficient ordinary-depth threshold

    sigma_c=Gamma/(Gamma+H_c)

lies strictly between Gamma and1/2. This is a genuine asymmetric-
middle class. For instance, if K contains a centrally symmetric
core of volume at least2sigma_c|K|, its actual core center supplies
the required ordinary-depth bound, regardless of the extra shape.
No unspecified stability constant is used.

For an exact planar failure of the volume-only certificate below
half-depth, take B=K any area-one triangle centered at its centroid,
and A=B/2. Then a=1/4,k_b=b=1, midpoint3B/4 subset K, and the
ordinary maximal depth of K is sigma=4/9. Indeed every triangle
point has a barycentric coordinate at least1/3; the corresponding
vertex cap through it has area at most(2/3)^2, while Grunbaum gives
the reverse bound at the centroid. Formula (11), together
with the larger endpoint centroid bound, certifies only

    (48sqrt(5)-91)/36 < 1/2
        =(Gamma_2/2)(1+1/4+1).

The strict inequality is equivalent to11520<11881. The positive
residual branch is valid because11520>11449. This is an actual
compatible volume/depth menu, but not an actual depth failure:
at the common centroid, K contributes4/9 and at least one endpoint
centroid lies in every through-source cap, contributing at least
Gamma_2|A|=1/9. Thus that actual point has raw depth at least5/9,
strictly above1/2. The missing information is the directional relation
of the endpoint traces, which is discarded by (11)-(12).

## 8. Retaining the endpoint ratio gives a sharp planar ordinary-depth threshold

There is a stronger planar conclusion when the actual endpoint ratio
a=|A|/|B| is retained rather than minimized out. Define, for0<a<=1,

    sigma_*(a)=4/[9(1-a)]                 if a<=1/9,
               2(5+2sqrt(a)+5a)/
                 [17+18sqrt(a)+17a]       if a>=1/9.  (14)

The values agree at a=1/9, where sigma_*=1/2. Everywhere else
sigma_*<1/2, and always sigma_*>=4/9. If an actual point of K has
ordinary normalized depth at least sigma_*(a), it and the centroid
of the larger endpoint supply the planar OC bound for EVERY compatible
middle area. In particular this covers genuinely asymmetric middles
having a sufficiently large symmetric core, with explicit constants.
At a=4/25, the threshold is330/673<1/2.

For clarity, (14) is the exact threshold for the two lower certificates
consisting of own ordinary depth plus residual BM, and the larger
endpoint's Grunbaum depth, uniformly over all positive middle areas.
This is not an extremal claim about actual bodies with a prescribed
ordinary depth, nor a claim that a smaller ordinary depth cannot pay
the target using additional directional information.

Here is the proof. Normalize b=1 and write k=|K|/b. If a<=1/9 and
sigma>=4/[9(1-a)], the larger endpoint covers k<=1-a, whereas the
own middle contribution sigma k covers k>=1-a. The two comparisons
follow by substituting k=1-a and observing their affine slopes.
No residual credit is needed in this range.

Now put x=sqrt(a) in[1/3,1],

    D=17+18x+17x^2,
    sigma=2(5+2x+5x^2)/D,
    v=(1+x)^2/4.

It suffices to use this sigma even if the actual point has greater
ordinary depth. Elementary algebra gives

    1-sigma=7(1+x)^2/D,
    1/2-sigma=(3x-1)(3-x)/(2D),
    sigma-4/9=2(11x^2-18x+11)/(9D)>0.

The endpoint alone pays the target when k<=k_l=1-x^2. The own
middle contribution pays it when

    k>=k_u=Gamma_2(1+x^2)/(2sigma-Gamma_2)=D/28.

Their possible gap is an actual bounded interval, because

    k_u-k_l=(3x-1)(15x+11)/28>=0.                   (15)

At its upper endpoint, (1-sigma)k_u=v and the residual payment is
zero. The own contribution equals the target there exactly. On the
whole interval[k_l,k_u], the residual-plus-own certificate is

    L(k)=sigma k+x^2-(2sqrt((1-sigma)k)-1)_+^2.    (16)

There is no missing outer positive part: the subtracted square is
at most x^2 because (1-sigma)k<=v. The function
(2sqrt(h)-1)_+^2 is convex in h>=0. It vanishes up to h=1/4; on
the other side its derivative is4-2/sqrt(h), increasing from zero.
Consequently L(k) minus the affine OC target is concave in k.
It remains to check the lower endpoint.

Put h_l=(1-sigma)(1-x^2). Direct factorization gives

    4D-63(1+x)^2(1-x^2)
       =(3x-1)(21x^3+49x^2+39x-5)>=0,

so0<=h_l<=4/9. If h_l<=1/4, then L(k_l)=1-h_l>=3/4>4/9.
Otherwise

    L(k_l)=4sqrt(h_l)-5h_l >=4/9.

The last inequality follows by factoring the difference, with
r=sqrt(h_l) in[1/2,2/3], as

    4r-5r^2-4/9=(2/3-r)(5r-2/3)>=0.

The target at k_l is exactly4/9. Thus both endpoints of the concave
gap are nonnegative, proving the target on the entire interval and
hence for every k. This includes the transition h_l=1/4 and the
collapsed interval at x=1/3.

Finally, the threshold is algebraically necessary for this certificate
family. For x>1/3, keep k=k_u from (15) but decrease sigma. The
missed-area parameter becomes larger than v, so residual credit is
zero. The own contribution is now strictly below target, while the
endpoint contribution is also below target since k_u>1-a.
For0<x<=1/3, at sigma_*=Gamma_2/(1-a) and k=1-a the missed area
is5/9-a, and

    4(5/9-a)-(1+sqrt(a))^2
       =(1-3x)(15x+11)/9>=0.

Decreasing sigma therefore makes the residual credit zero near this
middle area. Taking k just larger than1-a makes both the endpoint
and own certificates strictly less than target. These k values exceed
the whole-body BM minimum v, so the scalar obstruction is not caused
by violating that necessary volume restriction.

Thus (14) describes a precise ratio-dependent gain from choosing an
actual ordinary center, while the arbitrary-shape directional problem
below that threshold remains outside the present proof.
